title: MODULE 10 — Production Backend, Deployment and Observability

overview.text: Module objective: Understand how to transform a backend application that works on a developer's computer into a reliable, secure, deployable and observable production system.
Building a backend API is only one part of backend engineering.
Imagine you have completed the PrepSpaces course management API using Java, Spring Boot and PostgreSQL.
Now imagine deploying it for real students.
How will the application connect to the production database?
How will credentials be configured securely?
What happens when the application crashes?
How will updates be deployed without unnecessary downtime?
What happens when database connections are exhausted?
How will you know when the application becomes slow?
How will you identify which service caused a failed request?
How will you investigate an incident at 2 AM?
These problems belong to production backend engineering.
The objective of this module is to teach you how to operate backend applications as real services, not merely write code that works locally.
The production environment we will build
We will continue using the same technology stack from Modules 08 and 09:
These technologies demonstrate the major production engineering concepts. You do not need to deploy every application on Kubernetes or adopt every observability tool immediately.

blocks.text: An environment is a separate configuration and execution context in which an application runs.
During backend development, the application does not always interact with the same database, credentials, services or infrastructure.
For example, your local application might connect to a local PostgreSQL database, while the deployed application connects to a managed production database.
Software projects commonly maintain three important environments:
Developers write code, test features and identify defects.
Test the release candidate in a production-like environment.
Run the verified application and protect real application data.
The development environment is where developers implement and experiment with new features.
Imagine you are developing the enrollment functionality.
Spring Boot: localhost:8080 PostgreSQL: localhost:5432 Frontend: localhost:5173
The backend connects to the local database and uses test records.
spring: datasource: url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/course_dev username: dev_user password: ${DEV_DB_PASSWORD} jpa: show-sql: true logging: level: root: INFO com.example.course: DEBUG
SQL visibility helps developers understand database interactions.
Debug logs help identify application errors.
Local databases permit disposable test data.
Development credentials should not provide access to production systems.
Important: Debugging features must be controlled carefully. They should not accidentally expose sensitive information.
Staging is an environment used to verify a release candidate before it reaches production.
However, a local environment may differ from the deployed system.
The production database version may differ.
The application might not have permission to access object storage.
A reverse proxy might be configured incorrectly.
Staging helps discover these problems before release.
A staging environment should reproduce the important production characteristics:
Staging must not use production credentials.
Also, never casually copy real student records into staging. Use synthetic data or properly sanitized data with suitable access controls.
Production is where the application serves real users and handles real business operations.
A production failure can affect real users.
The application must also be configured to avoid exposing sensitive internal information.
Spring Boot supports environment-specific configuration through profiles.
The common configuration belongs in application.yml.
spring: jpa: show-sql: true logging: level: com.example.course: DEBUG
spring: jpa: show-sql: false logging: level: root: INFO com.example.course: INFO server: shutdown: graceful
Spring Boot profiles allow environment-specific configuration while keeping the application code largely the same.
A developer runs a testing script that deletes course records.
If the development application accidentally connects to the production database, real student information could be destroyed.
Key takeaway: Development is for building, staging is for release verification, and production is for serving real users. Never treat production as a testing playground.
Production configuration is the collection of settings that control how the backend application operates after deployment.
The same Java application can run in several environments with different configuration values.
Development Database: localhost Port: 8080 Logging: DEBUG Staging Database: staging-db Port: 8080 Logging: INFO Production Database: production-db Port: 8080 Logging: INFO
The application code does not necessarily need to change. Its environment determines its configuration.
One important principle is to separate application logic from environment-specific settings.
This makes the application dependent on hardcoded environment values.
@Configuration @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.database") public record DatabaseSettings( String host, String name, String username, String password ) {}
The values can be provided externally.
spring: datasource: url: ${DB_URL} username: ${DB_USERNAME} password: ${DB_PASSWORD} server: port: ${SERVER_PORT:8080}
The application receives database connection settings from its deployment environment.
The password above is a placeholder, not an actual production value.
Spring Boot's external configuration system supports environment-based overrides and structured configuration binding.
Do not commit real values into source code or Git repositories.
For a production environment, use an approved secret-management system or the deployment platform's protected secret injection mechanism.
Avoid exposing them through diagnostic endpoints.
This connects directly to Module 09's secrets and credential management lesson.
A practical production configuration could be:

server: port: 8080 shutdown: graceful spring: application: name: course-management-api datasource: url: ${DB_URL} username: ${DB_USERNAME} password: ${DB_PASSWORD} hikari: maximum-pool-size: 20 minimum-idle: 5 connection-timeout: 30000 jpa: open-in-view: false hibernate: ddl-auto: validate flyway: enabled: true management: endpoints: web: exposure: include: health,info,metrics,prometheus
This is an illustrative configuration. Pool size, timeouts and endpoint exposure must be chosen for your deployment. Secure the management endpoints through network restrictions and access controls.
Defines the HTTP port used by the application.
Allows the server to stop accepting new work and complete in-flight requests during a shutdown period.
Defines the maximum number of database connections managed by the application's connection pool.
Asks Hibernate to validate mapped entities against the existing schema rather than automatically creating or modifying the production schema.
Avoids keeping the persistence context open throughout the web request. This encourages explicit data retrieval and avoids certain database access surprises during response serialization.
Enabled at the appropriate infrastructure boundary
Key takeaway: Production configuration should be externally managed, environment-specific, validated and protected.
During development, you may run your Spring Boot application directly through an IDE such as IntelliJ IDEA.
src/main/java/ CourseController.java CourseService.java CourseRepository.java src/main/resources/ application.yml pom.xml
But a production server does not need your entire development workspace.
It needs a deployable application artifact and the runtime dependencies required to execute it.
Application packaging converts source code and dependencies into a distributable format.
For a Spring Boot application, a common deployment artifact is an executable JAR file.
You can package the project using Maven:
This JAR contains the application and its packaged runtime dependencies in the format produced by Spring Boot's Maven plugin.
This is useful because the packaged backend can run outside the developer's IDE.
A typical Maven build has several stages.
Execute applicable checks and verification steps.
Store the approved build artifact in a suitable artifact or container registry.
The following command runs the Maven lifecycle through verification:
This is generally preferable to blindly deploying a JAR built using a development-only command.
Imagine a developer creates a JAR today and deploys it.
Another developer builds the same project next week and gets a different result.
A production build should be traceable and reproducible as far as practical.
Track dependencies in Maven or Gradle.
Build from a specific Git commit.
Generate a software bill of materials (SBOM) where appropriate.
A particularly important production practice is promoting the same tested artifact through environments.
Git commit | v CI build | v JAR / Container Image | v Development verification | v Staging verification | v Production deployment
The artifact should not be rebuilt independently for production with different source code.
Ideally, the same container image digest verified in staging is the one promoted into production.
This helps eliminate differences between what was tested and what was released.
Your backend should have an identifiable release version.
A versioning convention such as Semantic Versioning can be useful:
Also record the Git commit or release identifier associated with each deployment.
This becomes valuable during incident investigation and rollback.
Key takeaway: Production deployment begins with a tested, traceable, versioned application artifact—not with copying a developer's project folder to a server.
Docker allows developers to package applications and their required runtime components into portable container images.
Imagine your backend works perfectly on your laptop.
You transfer it to a cloud server, but it fails because:
Docker helps reduce these environment differences by packaging the application into a container image.
These two technologies provide application isolation but operate differently.
Virtual machines generally provide a separate guest operating system environment.
Containers isolate applications while sharing the host operating system kernel.
Containers are usually lighter than full virtual machines, although their isolation and security properties are different.
Before containerizing the backend, understand these terms.
Instructions used to build an image
Persists data outside a container's writable layer
Exposes a container port through the host
A Dockerfile describes how to construct an application image.
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre WORKDIR /app COPY target/course-management-api.jar app.jar EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
Here it provides a Java 21 runtime environment.
Sets the working directory inside the container.
Documents the port used by the application.
It does not automatically publish that port to the host.
Defines the process executed when the container starts.
A better production approach separates the application build environment from the runtime environment.
A build environment needs Maven and a JDK.
A production container generally needs only the Java runtime and packaged application.
Docker multi-stage builds allow the final image to contain only the necessary runtime components.

# Stage 1: Build application FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build WORKDIR /app COPY pom.xml . RUN mvn dependency:go-offline COPY src ./src RUN mvn clean package -DskipTests # Stage 2: Runtime application FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre WORKDIR /app COPY --from=build /app/target/course-management-api.jar app.jar EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

This example assumes that the JAR name matches the application build configuration. For a production build, tests must run in CI before the image is published; the Docker build itself should not be treated as the only test gate.
The build stage includes tools that the running application does not need.
The final image does not need to contain:
This can reduce image size and reduce unnecessary software inside the runtime container.
Containers commonly run as root unless configured otherwise.
Running an application as root can increase the consequences of a container compromise.
A hardened runtime Dockerfile can create a dedicated user:

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre WORKDIR /app RUN groupadd --system appgroup \ && useradd --system \ --gid appgroup \ --no-create-home appuser COPY --chown=appuser:appgroup \ target/course-management-api.jar app.jar USER appuser EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
The application now runs as a restricted operating-system user rather than root.
Docker documents the default root-user behaviour and the USER instruction used to select a different identity.
docker run -d \ --name course-api \ -p 8080:8080 \ -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \ -e DB_URL="$DB_URL" \ -e DB_USERNAME="$DB_USERNAME" \ -e DB_PASSWORD="$DB_PASSWORD" \ course-management-api:1.0.0
The variables must be supplied from a secure environment. Do not put actual production passwords in shell scripts, Dockerfiles or committed Compose files.
A backend generally requires more than one service.
For development or a controlled lab environment, Docker Compose can run:

services: postgres: image: postgres:16 environment: POSTGRES_DB: course_db POSTGRES_USER: course_user POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD} volumes: - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data healthcheck: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U course_user -d course_db"] interval: 10s timeout: 5s retries: 5 backend: image: course-management-api:1.0.0 ports: - "8080:8080" environment: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod DB_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/course_db DB_USERNAME: course_user DB_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD} depends_on: postgres: condition: service_healthy volumes: postgres_data:
Create a local .env file for the lab:

Keep that file out of Git. For production, prefer an external secrets manager or the platform's secret mechanism. The Compose sample is for learning and is not a complete production security configuration.
Do not use docker compose down -v unless you intend to delete the persistent database volume.
Suppose PostgreSQL runs inside a container and the container is removed.
Without persistent storage, its database files may be lost.
Docker volumes allow database data to persist independently of the container lifecycle.
This is why the example includes:
In real production systems, a managed PostgreSQL service is often preferable to operating the primary database inside the same Compose deployment as the backend.
Key takeaway: Docker packages your application consistently. Images should be small, versioned, built from trusted dependencies and run with restricted privileges.
Deployment architecture describes how an application and its supporting infrastructure are arranged in a running environment.
A development application might run as a single Java process.
The goal is to operate the application reliably, securely and at the required scale.
Request routing, TLS termination and traffic distribution
This is a common production architecture pattern. It does not require two backend instances for every application; the number of instances depends on traffic, availability and budget requirements.
A reverse proxy sits between clients and backend servers.
Instead of exposing every backend instance directly, clients communicate through the proxy.
api.prepspaces.com | v Reverse Proxy | +---- Spring Boot Instance 1 | +---- Spring Boot Instance 2
Common reverse proxy and traffic-routing technologies include Nginx, HAProxy and cloud load balancers.
A load balancer distributes incoming requests among available application instances.
Imagine there are two backend servers:
The load balancer distributes requests between them.
If Instance 1 becomes unhealthy, the load balancer should stop sending it normal traffic, according to its health-check configuration.
This can improve availability and help scale application traffic.
However, adding more backend instances does not automatically solve every performance issue.
A backend instance is easier to scale when it does not depend on local memory for shared user state.
If the backend stores user sessions only in Instance 1's local memory, a request routed to Instance 2 may not recognize the session.
A more scalable approach uses appropriately designed stateless authentication or shared session storage.
For course progress and user records, PostgreSQL remains the persistent source of truth in this example.
Increase the resources of one server.
2 CPU cores, 4 GB RAM | v 8 CPU cores, 16 GB RAM
Increase the number of application instances.
1 Spring Boot instance | v 3 Spring Boot instances
Adds resources to an existing server
May have a larger single failure domain
When releasing a new backend version, you should choose how the update reaches users.
Stop the old version, then start the new version.
Old: Instance 1 + Instance 2 + Instance 3 Step 1: Update Instance 1 Step 2: Update Instance 2 Step 3: Update Instance 3 New: Instance 1 + Instance 2 + Instance 3
This can reduce downtime, provided that old and new versions can safely coexist during the deployment.
Test the green environment and switch traffic after verification.
Rollback can involve switching traffic back to blue, provided the database and other shared changes remain compatible.
Release the new version to a small percentage of traffic.
Observe error rates, latency and application behaviour before increasing traffic.
Important: Deployment strategy is not just about replacing containers. Database schema changes, background jobs, API compatibility and session handling must also be considered.
6.1 Why is production database management different?
During development, developers frequently modify database tables.
For example, your original courses table might contain:
courses ------- id title description level created_at updated_at
In development, you may delete the database and recreate it.
In production, that is not acceptable.
You must modify the database while protecting existing data.
This is the purpose of database migration management.
A database migration is a controlled, versioned change to a database schema or its data.
Instead of modifying the database manually, developers create migration scripts and track them in version control.
A database migration tool that manages and tracks schema changes through versioned migration scripts.
Flyway allows developers to define how a database should evolve across environments.
src/main/resources/ db/ migration/ V1__create_courses_table.sql V2__create_students_table.sql V3__create_enrollments_table.sql V4__add_course_level.sql V5__create_course_progress_index.sql
The naming convention identifies the migration version and description.
When Flyway runs, it checks which migrations have been applied and executes applicable pending migrations.
It maintains a schema history table containing migration information, including checksums and execution status.
CREATE TABLE courses ( id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL, description TEXT, created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP );
CREATE TABLE students ( id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL, email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE );

CREATE TABLE enrollments ( id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, student_id BIGINT NOT NULL, course_id BIGINT NOT NULL, enrolled_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CONSTRAINT fk_student FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(id), CONSTRAINT fk_course FOREIGN KEY (course_id) REFERENCES courses(id), CONSTRAINT unique_student_course UNIQUE (student_id, course_id) );
These scripts define the database structure in a repeatable way.
6.5 Why should migration files be immutable?
Flyway executes the script and records its checksum.
Later, a developer edits the same file to include another column.
Now the migration on disk differs from the migration already applied to the database.
Do not edit migrations that have already been applied in shared environments.
Create a new migration for every subsequent schema modification.
Test migrations against realistic database versions and data volumes.
Flyway's validation checks migration names, types and checksums to detect inconsistencies.
Add the Flyway dependency and PostgreSQL database support to your Maven project.
Use the PostgreSQL-specific Flyway module required by your chosen Flyway version when applicable, and keep it compatible with your Spring Boot dependency management.
spring: flyway: enabled: true locations: classpath:db/migration jpa: hibernate: ddl-auto: validate
Avoid using Hibernate schema auto-update as the production database migration strategy.
A safe release pipeline should look like this:
For a production database, a separate, controlled migration job is often preferable to allowing every newly started application instance to attempt migrations independently.
The deployment should ensure that only one migration process runs against the target database at a time and that the application version being released is compatible with the schema.
This is particularly important when the backend must remain available during deployment.
You want to replace it with:
If older application instances are still running, they may continue requesting title and fail.
A safer approach is the expand-and-contract pattern.
Deploy code capable of handling the transition. New code should read the new field, and writes must keep both representations synchronized as required during compatibility.
Confirm that the new application version and migrated data work correctly.
After all old application versions have been retired and the compatibility window has passed, remove the old column in a later deployment.
Old Schema | v Expand Schema | v Migrate Existing Data | v Deploy Compatible Application | v Verify | v Remove Obsolete Schema
This approach reduces the risk of incompatible application and database versions during rolling deployments.
Every request that accesses PostgreSQL may need a database connection.
Creating an entirely new connection for every database operation is expensive.
Connection pooling maintains a reusable collection of connections.
Spring Boot Application | v HikariCP | +---- Connection 1 +---- Connection 2 +---- Connection 3 +---- Connection 4 | v PostgreSQL
Time waiting to obtain a connection
Backend instances: 3 Maximum connections per instance: 20
Now imagine your database has a connection budget of 80.
Therefore, pool sizing must be coordinated with the database's actual connection capacity.
Increasing the pool size without understanding database limits can make production performance worse.
A migration strategy is incomplete without a recovery strategy.
How much data loss, measured in time, can the business tolerate?
Example: An RPO of 15 minutes means the objective is to limit data loss to approximately the previous 15 minutes of activity.
How quickly should the service be restored after a disruption?
Example: An RTO of 1 hour means the objective is to restore the service within approximately one hour.
A backup is not a reliable recovery plan until restoration has been tested.
Key takeaway: Production database management requires controlled migrations, compatible application releases, connection planning, backups and tested recovery procedures.
A health check is a mechanism used to determine whether an application or service is operating in an acceptable state.
Imagine your Spring Boot backend container is running.
Does this prove that the API is healthy?
The process may be alive while:
The HTTP server is unable to process requests.
A running process is not necessarily a healthy service.
Provides production-oriented endpoints for application health, metrics and operational information.
Actuator can expose application health through:
A healthy response may look like:
The actual response may include additional components depending on configuration and security.
management: endpoints: web: exposure: include: health,info,metrics,prometheus
This exposes the selected management endpoints over HTTP when configured and available.
Do not expose all management endpoints publicly. Use network restrictions and appropriate authorization controls.
There are three particularly important health concepts.
Is the application process alive and able to continue operating?
Imagine the Java process becomes permanently stuck.
A failed liveness check can trigger a restart under an orchestrator that supports this behaviour.
However, a liveness probe should not fail just because PostgreSQL is temporarily unavailable.
If PostgreSQL goes down, every backend instance might fail its liveness check and restart continuously.
This can make recovery even worse.
Is this instance ready to receive application traffic?
Imagine the application container has started but has not yet finished initialization.
It should not receive normal requests until it is ready.
A failed readiness check can cause the platform to stop routing traffic to that instance without necessarily restarting it.
Has the application completed its initial startup process?
This is especially useful for applications with slow initialization.
It prevents readiness and liveness checks from treating a still-starting process as an application failure.
Kubernetes explicitly distinguishes startup, liveness and readiness probes because each serves a different operational purpose.
A Spring Boot application can expose dedicated endpoints for liveness and readiness.
management: endpoint: health: probes: enabled: true group: liveness: include: livenessState readiness: include: readinessState
When application availability state is enabled, Spring Boot provides health information that can be used by container orchestration platforms.
Liveness should measure the application's own ability to make progress.
Readiness may incorporate required dependency availability, but only when that dependency is genuinely necessary to serve requests.
Do not indiscriminately make every optional external service part of readiness.
Spring Boot provides dedicated health groups for Kubernetes liveness and readiness probes.

containers: - name: course-api image: course-management-api:1.0.0 ports: - containerPort: 8080 startupProbe: httpGet: path: /actuator/health/liveness port: 8080 periodSeconds: 10 failureThreshold: 30 livenessProbe: httpGet: path: /actuator/health/liveness port: 8080 periodSeconds: 10 readinessProbe: httpGet: path: /actuator/health/readiness port: 8080 periodSeconds: 5
This is a simplified example. You must also configure probe tolerances, application startup characteristics and access to management endpoints appropriately.
A graceful shutdown means stopping an application without unnecessarily interrupting work that is already in progress.
Imagine a student submits an enrollment request.
Now imagine the deployment system terminates the container while the operation is running.
An abrupt shutdown can interrupt requests and create errors.
server: shutdown: graceful spring: lifecycle: timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 20s
The timeout defines how long the application lifecycle waits for shutdown operations in the relevant phase.
Spring Boot supports graceful shutdown with its embedded web servers and documents a configurable shutdown grace period.
Mark the instance as unavailable for new traffic.
Let ongoing requests complete within the shutdown window.
Verify that the replacement instance is ready.
You should ensure the container's termination grace period is long enough for the application's configured shutdown timeout and any required platform delays.
For Kubernetes, the pod termination grace period and lifecycle hooks must be coordinated with Spring Boot's shutdown configuration.
Key takeaway: Health checks tell the platform whether an application can operate or receive requests. Graceful shutdown helps the application finish work safely when it is being replaced or stopped.
Structured logging means recording application events in a consistent, machine-readable format rather than writing arbitrary text messages.
Imagine your backend receives a course enrollment request.
A traditional log might look like:
Student enrollment was successful for course 10
This is understandable to a human, but difficult for monitoring systems to search reliably across thousands of events.
A structured log records information in separate fields.
Now a logging platform can easily search:
Events generated by a particular service.
Events associated with a specific request.
Production applications can generate millions of log entries.
Consistency: Every event follows a defined format.
Searchability: Fields can be filtered and queried.
Correlation: Events from different services can be associated with the same request.
Automation: Monitoring systems can detect specific event patterns.
Investigation: Developers can reconstruct what happened during an incident.
A good backend log event might contain:
Do not add sensitive information merely because the logging format supports arbitrary fields. User identity fields should also be minimized or pseudonymized where appropriate.
Backend applications commonly use these logging levels:
Production logging typically uses INFO as a baseline, with WARN and ERROR for important operational events.
DEBUG and TRACE should be enabled selectively and only with suitable safeguards.
8.5 Implementing structured logging in Spring Boot
Spring Boot applications commonly use SLF4J with Logback.

@Service @Slf4j public class EnrollmentService { public void enroll(Long studentId, Long courseId) { log.info( "Enrollment requested: studentId={}, courseId={}", studentId, courseId ); // Business operation log.info( "Enrollment completed: studentId={}, courseId={}", studentId, courseId ); } }
The example uses Lombok's @Slf4j annotation. You can alternatively create an SLF4J logger directly.
To produce JSON logs, use a compatible structured logging implementation or encoder.
Modern Spring Boot versions also provide structured logging support through supported logging configurations. Select the format and fields based on your Spring Boot version and logging backend.
Imagine an API request travels through:
Frontend | v API Gateway | v Course Service | v Enrollment Service | v Database
You want to find all events associated with this one request.
A correlation ID allows you to associate the related logs.
The same ID is included in the application logs associated with that request.
This helps connect events that would otherwise appear unrelated.
In a distributed application, trace IDs and span IDs provide an even richer mechanism for following operations across services.
Structured logging must follow the security principles from Module 09.
Also implement log rotation or centralized retention policies.
A container's local writable filesystem should not be the only location where important production logs are stored.
Key takeaway: Structured logging transforms application messages into searchable operational data, making it much easier to diagnose production problems.
This lesson introduces two essential observability techniques.
Before understanding them, we need to understand a broader concept: observability.
Observability is the ability to understand the internal behaviour of a system by examining the information it produces.
Imagine your PrepSpaces API suddenly becomes slow.
Users report that course pages take 10 seconds to load.
You know something is wrong, but you do not know where the problem exists.
Observability provides information that helps you investigate these conditions.
Where did the request spend time?
Metrics show numerical trends over time.
Traces show the path and timing of individual operations.
Metrics are numerical measurements collected over time.
CPU utilization: 75% Memory usage: 1.8 GB Active requests: 120 HTTP error rate: 2% Database connections: 18
Metrics help detect changes in system behaviour.
How many requests your backend receives.
A sudden increase might indicate a traffic spike.
How long requests take to complete.
These percentiles help identify slow requests that averages might hide.
How much processing capacity the server is consuming.
How much memory the application is consuming.
How many connections are active, idle or waiting.
How often the JVM performs garbage collection and how much time it consumes.
Collects time-series metrics from monitored applications and infrastructure.
Prometheus commonly collects metrics by periodically scraping HTTP endpoints.
Spring Boot Application | v /actuator/prometheus | v Prometheus Server | v Time-Series Metrics Storage
To expose the Prometheus metrics endpoint, add the appropriate Micrometer Prometheus registry dependency to the Spring Boot application.
For example, with a compatible Spring Boot 3.x or 4.x setup:
management: endpoints: web: exposure: include: health,info,prometheus
Prometheus can collect metrics exposed through:
This endpoint should be accessible only to your monitoring infrastructure, not unnecessarily exposed to the public internet.
Displays monitoring data through dashboards, charts, alerts and operational visualizations.
For example, a backend dashboard could show:
Illustrative request volume over ten time intervals.
Sample dashboard values, not live PrepSpaces measurements.
A production dashboard should help engineers understand application behaviour at a glance.
Now imagine a course API request passes through multiple services.
Frontend | v API Gateway | v Course Service | +---- Enrollment Service | | | v | PostgreSQL | +---- Notification Service | v Email Provider
A simple application log might tell you that the request took four seconds overall.
Distributed tracing breaks the request into smaller operations called spans.
Now you know that the external email provider was responsible for most of the delay.
Trace: The entire journey of one request through the system.
Span: An individual operation within that journey.
Conceptual visualization; spans may overlap in parallel execution and therefore need not add up exactly to total wall-clock duration.
Provides APIs, SDKs and instrumentation for collecting and exporting logs, metrics and distributed traces.
OpenTelemetry provides a common instrumentation approach across services.
It helps collect telemetry and send it to compatible observability platforms.
The Java ecosystem includes stable support for all three telemetry signal types, according to its current documentation.
Suppose an API gateway creates a trace.
When the request moves to another backend service, the trace context should travel with it.
This helps ensure the operations appear in the same distributed trace.
Common propagation mechanisms include W3C Trace Context headers such as:
Without proper context propagation, the tracing platform might display separate traces instead of one connected request journey.

Key takeaway: Observability is not just collecting logs. Metrics show trends, traces reveal request journeys, and logs explain events. Together they provide a much clearer picture of production behaviour.
Monitoring is the continuous observation of an application's health, performance and operational behaviour.
Monitoring helps you track known conditions and detect when something goes wrong.
Imagine PrepSpaces is serving thousands of course requests.
The database connection pool becomes nearly full.
Without monitoring, these problems may remain unnoticed until users complain.
With monitoring, the engineering team can receive an alert when important conditions exceed defined thresholds.
A professional backend monitoring strategy covers several areas.
An alert is a notification generated when a monitored condition requires attention.
Condition: API error rate > 5% Duration: 5 consecutive minutes Severity: Critical Action: Notify the backend engineering team
Alerts should be based on symptoms that matter to users and operators, not every small fluctuation in the infrastructure.
Detect when an application is unavailable.
Course API is returning failed health checks.
Detect an increase in failed operations.
CPU remains above an operational threshold.
Memory utilization approaches the container limit.
Detect suspicious operational activity, such as:
Do not automatically classify every failed login as an attack. Alert thresholds should account for ordinary user mistakes and background noise.
Prometheus supports alert rules that evaluate metric expressions.

groups: - name: course-api-alerts rules: - alert: HighApiErrorRate expr: | ( sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{ status=~"5.." }[5m])) / clamp_min( sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m])), 0.001 ) ) > 0.05 for: 5m labels: severity: critical annotations: summary: High backend API error rate description: More than 5% of requests are returning 5xx errors.
The example assumes the application exports a suitable HTTP server request metric with the indicated name and labels.
for: How long the condition must persist.
Prometheus documents alert rules and the role of the for duration in avoiding alerts for conditions that disappear immediately.
Alert fatigue occurs when engineers receive too many unimportant notifications.
Imagine your system sends 300 alerts per day.
Eventually, engineers may stop responding carefully to notifications.
Remove alerts that do not lead to useful action.
Document how to investigate every critical alert.
These concepts are important in production engineering.
The percentage of successful API requests.
99.9% of eligible API requests should succeed over a defined 30-day window.
A formal agreement with customers that may include availability commitments and consequences when they are not met.
These are example values, not a recommendation to promise 99.9% availability before you can measure and support it.
If your monthly availability target is 99.9%, the theoretical error budget for a 30-day month is:
This is the amount of downtime represented by the 0.1% failure allowance under that particular availability definition.
Error budgets help engineering teams balance reliability improvements against feature development.
They also encourage teams to make release decisions based on observed reliability rather than assumptions.
Grafana supports alerting based on Prometheus metrics, allowing teams to detect conditions and route notifications through configured contact points.
Key takeaway: Monitoring measures system behaviour continuously. Alerting informs engineers when an important condition requires investigation or intervention.
Every backend application requires computing resources to operate.
A backend can become slow or unavailable when one of these resources becomes exhausted.
Imagine your API receives many simultaneous requests.
Each request may consume memory, execute Java code, access PostgreSQL and call other services.
As traffic increases, resource demand increases too.
Resource management is about controlling this demand and ensuring that the application does not exceed its available capacity.
CPU is responsible for processing application instructions.
A Spring Boot application uses CPU for:
Normal CPU usage: 25% After traffic increase: 95%
The application may experience increased response latency because CPU resources are heavily utilized.
Do not assume that increasing CPU is always the correct fix. First identify what consumes it.
A simplified JVM memory model contains:
Imagine an API loads thousands of course records into memory.
If the application retains too many objects unnecessarily, memory usage can grow.
Container termination due to memory limits.
A JVM may be configured with a heap limit:
These are example settings, not universal production values.
In a container, the total memory limit must account for more than Java heap alone. Native memory, thread stacks, direct buffers and other process memory also consume the container's allocation.
A container may be restricted to specific resource limits.
This limits the container's memory to 1 GB and its CPU allocation to approximately 1.5 CPUs.
Docker resource constraints help prevent one application from consuming unlimited host resources.
However, a container being limited does not mean the application has been properly sized.
You must test the actual workload under those limits.
Now suppose 20 requests are using connections simultaneously.
It must wait for a connection to become available, or eventually time out.
Multiple application instances collectively exceeding database capacity.
A thread is a unit of execution.
Spring Boot uses threads to process incoming requests and perform application work.
The thread pool is too small.
The application blocks threads for long periods.
Slow external services occupy request threads.
100 incoming requests | v Limited worker threads | +---- 20 executing | +---- 80 waiting
The backend might be alive, but requests will experience long delays.
SELECT * FROM courses ORDER BY created_at DESC;
If the table contains millions of records, retrieving everything can be expensive.
A better API may use pagination:
SELECT id, title, created_at FROM courses ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 0;
You may also need appropriate indexes depending on query patterns.
They increase storage use and can slow down writes. Always examine real query plans and actual database workload before adding indexes.
Do not randomly increase every server resource when an application becomes slow.
Is the problem high latency, 5xx errors, memory usage or downtime?
Review metrics, resource graphs, application health and alerts.
Use traces to identify the slow service or operation.
Find exceptions, timeouts and related events.
Check CPU, memory, threads, database connections and disk.
Determine which component is responsible rather than treating only the symptom.
Test the change and monitor whether the incident is resolved.
Capacity planning means estimating the resources your system needs under expected workloads.
Concurrent users: 500 Average API requests per user: 2 per minute Estimated request rate: 500 × 2 / 60 = 16.67 requests per second
This is only an initial workload estimate.
You should measure the application under realistic load before deciding how much infrastructure to purchase.
Key takeaway: Performance problems are usually resource or workload problems. Measure first, identify the bottleneck, then optimize or scale the correct component.
A production incident is an unexpected event that negatively affects the availability, reliability, security or performance of a live application.
Imagine PrepSpaces has deployed a new backend version.
At 10:00 AM, the new release goes live.
Students report that courses are not loading.
Database connection usage reaches its maximum.
The engineering team's responsibility is to restore the service, minimize user impact, investigate the underlying problem and prevent recurrence.
Not every application problem has the same importance.
You should classify incidents according to their impact.
Entire platform unavailable or major active security compromise
Enrollment or authentication unavailable for many users
These severity levels are an example classification. Organizations should define their own impact and response requirements.
A professional incident response process typically follows these stages.
Monitoring, alerts or users identify an application problem.
Determine severity, affected users and affected services.
Analyze logs, metrics, traces, deployments and infrastructure.
Reduce user impact through rollback, traffic routing, disabling a broken feature or another controlled workaround.
Restore normal application behaviour and verify critical user workflows.
Implement permanent fixes and improve monitoring, testing and operational procedures.
Suppose your production API begins returning HTTP 500 errors.
ALERT: HighApiErrorRate Service: course-management-api Environment: production Error rate: 12% Normal target: Less than 1% Status: FIRING
Check whether the backend is running.
For example, PostgreSQL sessions can be inspected using:
SELECT state, COUNT(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state;
This provides a count of database sessions by state.
CPU: 45% Memory: 65% DB pool: 20 / 20 API p95: 4,000 ms Error rate: 12%
This indicates that database connection availability may be a key part of the failure.
It is evidence for investigation, not yet proof of the root cause.
Suppose the affected enrollment requests show:
HTTP Request | v Enrollment Service | v Course Repository | v PostgreSQL | v Connection Acquisition Timeout
The database connection pool is taking too long to provide connections.
Check whether a new release was deployed shortly before the problem started.
Correlate the incident timeline with deployment history.
Possible mitigation actions, depending on the evidence:
Roll back the problematic application release.
Disable a newly introduced non-essential feature.
Address a blocked or slow database operation.
Do not increase the connection pool blindly. That could exceed PostgreSQL's available connection capacity and make the incident worse.
Also test the important user workflows, not just the health endpoint.
Fixing the symptom does not necessarily fix the underlying problem.
Imagine your database connection pool became exhausted because an endpoint held transactions open while waiting for a slow external service.
Increasing the pool size may temporarily reduce the errors, but it does not address the architectural problem.
Root-cause analysis investigates the reason the system failed.
A common technique is the Five Whys method.
Why 1: The database connection pool became exhausted.
Why 2: Connections remained occupied for too long.
Why 3: A new service implementation performed slow external operations within a transaction.
Why 4: The service did not separate database work from external communication.
Why 5: Code review and performance testing did not include this integration pattern.
The corrective action should address the underlying design, not just the final visible failure.
A production incident should be documented.
Reduced transaction duration and added testing
After the issue has been resolved, conduct a post-incident review.
This should focus on improving the engineering system rather than blaming an individual developer.
Why did automated testing not identify it?
Why was the incident detected when it was?
The output should be a set of specific, assigned and trackable improvement actions.
Key takeaway: Production incident management is not simply restarting a failed server. It is a structured engineering process involving detection, investigation, mitigation, recovery and prevention.

08 — Backend Testing and API Quality Engineering
Can the application withstand unauthorized and malicious requests?
Can the application run reliably in production?
Consider a student enrolling in a PrepSpaces course:
Module 08: Verify that enrollment is created correctly and that duplicate enrollment is rejected.
Module 09: Ensure that students cannot enroll through unauthorized operations or modify another user's enrollment.
Module 10: Deploy the enrollment API, monitor its response time, detect failures and recover the service if a production problem occurs.
The central engineering principle of Module 10:
A backend application is not production-ready simply because its code compiles, its APIs work locally or its Docker container starts successfully.

A production-ready backend must be deployable, configurable, observable, recoverable and maintainable. Engineers must be able to understand what the application is doing, detect when it fails, investigate why it failed and restore normal service without unnecessarily compromising application data or user experience.
That is the difference between building a backend application and operating a production backend system.
